string.text: My liege, your banner flies over my hall as it flies over the realm. My riders and my sword are yours to command.
Well met again, my liege. My oath stands as firm as on the day I swore it, and the watch is kept.
Hail, traveller. From Fornost to Minas Tirith, those who stand against the Shadow have found courtesy among us, though I would know your purpose first.
Hail again. The roads have not grown kinder since we last met, so a friendly banner upon them is welcome.
You ride armed through lands held in the name of Elendil's heirs. State your business plainly and be brief.
So we meet again. I have not forgotten our last dealing, and I will be watching your hands while we speak.
Your banner is known to me, and it has never been a friend to this realm. Speak quickly, if you must speak at all.
You again. Every league you ride upon this soil is stolen, and I mean to see each one paid for.
Well met. It gladdens me to find one who keeps the old ways on these roads, for there are fewer of us with every passing year.
Well met again. Sit with me a while if you can; there is news from the North and the South both, and little of it good.
You have overstepped, and the law of this realm is plain. Lay down your arms and you will be held with honour until terms are made.
My company outnumbers yours many times over. Yield now, and no one need bleed for a quarrel that words could settle.
By the oath I swore to my realm, you will go no further. Throw down your weapons or be cut down where you stand.
You are surrounded, and I have little mercy to spare for the enemies of the West. Surrender, and you may yet live to see a cell.
It grieves me to raise steel against one of our own blood, yet my oath leaves me no other road. Yield, and I swear you will be treated with honour.
Stand down, I beg you. Our forebears did not cross the Sea so that their heirs might kill one another on a muddy road.
The day is yours. I yield, and I trust you to hold me by the customs of honourable war.
Then I leave in your debt, and I do not forget my debts, whatever comes between our banners.
I am beaten, and I yield my sword. Do as you will with me, but the West will remember this day.
I did not look for mercy from you. I will think on it, though it changes nothing between our realms.
Enough. I will spend no more lives of our own blood on this field, and I yield to you.
I hoped you would show the grace of our line, and you have. Go well, and may the old blood one day stand under a single banner again.
By your leave, my liege. I return to my post, and the watch goes on.
Fare well. May the Valar guard your road and bring you safe to your hearth.
We are done here. Ride on, and keep to the open road while you are in our lands.
Go. The beacons will burn for you before long.
Go safely. And whatever befalls, remember the White Tree and the kings who first planted it.
My liege, the riders of my éored are yours to command. Say where the Mark has need of us, and we will ride.
The oath I swore you still holds, my liege, and our horses are rested. We wait on your word.
Well met on the open plain. Those who cross the Mark in peace have no quarrel with us, and some find friends here.
Good to see your banner on the grasslands again. We have shared the road before, and I would gladly share it once more.
Rein in. You ride on the grass of the Riddermark, and I have not yet decided whether you are welcome on it.
You again. My riders remember your banner, and they do not count it among their friends.
You stand with the enemies of the Mark. Every rider here is sworn to drive you back the way you came.
So you dare return to our plains. My riders have not forgotten you, and their spears are sharp.
I knew you for a friend by the way you sit your horse. Ride with us a while; the plains are wide and the news is grim.
It does me good to see a friendly face out here. Share the ale skin and tell me what you have seen along the Entwash.
We have run you down, and no one outrides my éored on open ground. Lay down your arms and you will be treated fairly.
Your horses are spent and mine are fresh. Yield now, and no blood need be spilled between us today.
You have harried the Mark long enough. Throw down your weapons, or my riders will trample you into the grass.
By the blood of Eorl, you will not leave these plains armed. Yield, or face the charge.
I would rather share a saddle-skin of ale with you than a field of blood. Yield, and you will be dealt with honourably.
Enough. We grew up on the same grass under the same sky, and I would rather take your sword than your life. Give it to me.
The field is yours. I yield, and I trust you to keep the old customs of the plains.
You let me ride free. I will remember it, and so will my riders.
My horse is down and my riders are scattered. I yield, though it shames me before my forebears.
Mercy was the last thing I looked for from you. It settles nothing between us, but I will not forget it.
You rode better than I did today. I yield, and I am glad it was you who bested me and no stranger.
Free again, and by your hand. Should you ever need a spear at your side, send word to my hall.
By your leave, my liege. My riders await your call.
Good grass and clear skies on your road. Ride well.
Ride on, then, and keep your blades sheathed while you cross the Mark.
Go. When next we meet, our spears will be lowered for the charge.
Ride safe. There is always a seat for you at our fire, and a fresh horse in our stables.
My liege, well met on the road. The steadings are quiet and the granaries full, and my riders are yours to send where you will.
Good to see you again, my liege. Say the word and my spears go with you, as my oath bound them.
Well met. We have no quarrel with you, and the roads of the North are long enough for two companies to pass in peace.
You again, and on good terms still. Trade has gone well along the rivers this season, and I hope your road has treated you as well.
Hold there. I do not know you, and in these lands we like to know who rides armed past our steadings.
We have crossed paths before, and I have not forgotten how it went. Keep your hands where my archers can see them.
You ride under a banner that wishes ill on the free North. My bowstrings are strung and my riders are restless.
Back in our vales, are you? Your side has burned enough of our harvests, and I mean to see that you pay for them.
Well met, neighbour. It does me good to see a face from the river country out here on the road.
There you are again. Sit a while if you can spare it, there is bread and honey in the wagon and news from home.
You are outnumbered and far from help. Give up your arms and you will be treated fairly, as is our custom.
I would rather settle this with a fair bargain than with arrows. Yield now, and we can talk of ransom like sensible people.
You have trampled our fields long enough. Lay down your weapons, or my archers will empty their quivers into your ranks.
Every steading you burned has sent riders to my banner. Throw down your arms now, for I will not ask a second time.
My oath binds me to this, though it sits ill with me. Yield, and no blood of ours need be spilled today.
We are both children of the river and the wood, and I take no joy in this. Put up your sword and come quietly.
You have the better of me today. I yield, and I trust you to deal with me as fairly as I would have dealt with you.
You let me go without a ransom? That is a debt, and in the North we pay our debts.
My riders are broken and I will not waste the rest of them. I yield, though it sticks in my throat.
Free to go, am I? I will take it, but do not think one kindness buys back all the fields you burned.
Enough. I will not see more of our own laid in barrows over this quarrel. I yield to you.
You have a good heart, neighbour. When this feud is over, the first cup at my table is yours.
By your leave, my liege. May the road be dry and a warm hall wait for you at its end.
Fair winds and full barns to you. We will meet again at some market or other.
Go on your way, then. I will be watching which way it leads.
Get off our roads, and pray my scouts lose your trail.
Keep safe, neighbour, and keep the fire lit. The East is never as quiet as it looks.
The clans stand behind you, my chief. Point to where the horse-lords must pay, and my spears will go there.
My chief. The hill clans keep faith with you, and my warband waits on your word.
You come to us openly, so I will deal with you openly. Dunland keeps good faith with those who keep it first.
Back on our roads again. There is a place at our fires for a friend of the clans, so long as you stay one.
I do not know you, and in these hills a stranger is a thing to be watched. Speak, and keep your hand away from your sword.
You again. The clans have long memories, and mine holds nothing good of you yet.
You ride through hills that were ours before any horse-lord was born. Every step you take here is a debt I mean to collect.
I have not forgotten you, and neither have the graves of my clan. Say what you came to say.
Peat smoke on your cloak, the same as mine. Sit with me a while; the valley lords can wait for their reckoning.
Well met again. The fires in the high glens have burned low since you went away, and it is good to see a face from home.
My spears hem you in on three sides. Lay down your arms and you walk away from this alive.
The hills give one warning and no more. Yield now, or the crows settle the rest.
The horse-lords took our valleys and called it their right. By the same right I take you today, so throw down your weapons.
The White Hand promised these lands back to the clans, and you stand on them. Yield, or be buried in them.
The hills have enough of their own in the ground already. Yield, and you will be held as kin until this is settled.
We drank from the same streams, you and I. Give up your sword before I have to spill your blood into them.
Enough. My clan has bled for this day, and I yield to you. See that you treat us fairly.
Freed, with my sword back in my hand. I will think long on that before we meet again.
Take my sword, then. Dunland has lost battles before and still stands, and it will stand long after you.
You let me go. One kindness does not wash out the old wrongs, and the clans will not forget them.
You fought like one born in the high glens. I yield, and there is less shame in yielding to blood of the hills.
Blood answers to blood, it seems. I owe you a debt now, and the hills pay what they owe.
By your leave, my chief. The clans will be ready when you call.
Go safely through the hills. Keep to the open tracks, where my scouts can see you coming.
Go, then. And keep your distance from my hall.
Go. The clans will be waiting in every glen you cross.
Go well, and keep the old fires burning wherever the road takes you.
The sun rises on my sovereign. My spears and my house stand ready for your word.
Welcome again, my liege. The South is quiet under your hand, and I mean to keep it so.
You ride under no banner I have cause to hate. Speak plainly, and the South will hear you out.
Our paths cross again. You have kept faith with us so far, and I have kept count.
I know your banner, and I do not trust it. Say what you came to say, and keep your hand away from your sword.
You again. The sun is hot today and so is my temper, so choose your words with care.
The serpent banner bows to no stranger. You stand in the path of the South, and that is a poor place to stand.
I have not forgotten our last meeting. The South keeps its grudges as long as it keeps its oaths.
Well met under the same sun. It is good to see a face that knows the heat of home.
Again our roads meet, and I am glad of it. There is shade enough here for two who share a homeland.
You have strayed into the reach of the South, and my riders outnumber yours. Lay down your arms and I will be merciful.
Count my spears before you answer. Yield now, and you may yet see another sunrise.
Under the serpent banner there is no mercy for those who make war on the South. Throw down your blades, or the jackals will have you by nightfall.
The South has waited long for this day. Surrender and live in chains, or fight and die in the dust.
The sun will not shine on kin killing kin today if I can help it. Yield, and we settle this as kin.
We drink the same water and curse the same enemies, yet here we stand. Put up your weapons before blood is spilled between us.
I yield. Treat me fairly, and my house will remember it.
You open the gate and ask nothing. My house will weigh what that means.
My warriors lie in the dust, and I will not waste the rest. Take my sword, and take your victory.
You let me go, but do not mistake this for peace. When our banners meet again, I will not be the one in chains.
You fought like a true child of the sun. I yield to you, and there is no shame in it.
You have shown mercy as the old ways teach. I will remember it when the spears are raised again.
By your leave. May the sun favour your reign.
Go with the sun at your back, and may your road always find water.
Enough talk. Ride on before my patience wears any thinner.
Go, and count the days until the serpent finds you.
Farewell. May the South keep you safe until our roads cross again.
My oath is yours, and so is every rider under my banner. Say where the wagons should roll and we will roll.
You find my war-band ready, as I swore it would be. The horses are fed and the spears are sharp for your command.
Our banners are not crossed, so I will hear you. Speak plainly, as the steppe teaches.
We meet again on open ground, and still at peace. My riders will keep their bows unstrung while we talk.
I know your colours, and I do not trust them. My riders are watching your hands.
You again. The wind carries talk of you through every camp in the East, and little of it is kind.
A stranger who rides against my lord's cause. Choose your words well, for they may be your last.
We have crossed blades before, and my clan still counts that debt. Say what you came to say.
Welcome, child of the wide grass. Share my fire and my brew, as our clans have always done.
The road brings you back to my wagons. Sit, and tell me what news comes from the camps.
Your little band is ringed by my riders. Throw down your arms and I will remember you were sensible.
The war-horns have sounded and my spears are lowered. Yield to me now, or be trampled where you stand.
I swore an oath to break those who stand against my lord, and you stand in front of me. Kneel, or my chariots ride you down.
My riders have run you to ground like a lame colt. Give up your sword and your silver, or the crows will have the rest.
The war sets clan against clan, and I must follow it. Yield to me, and you will be treated with honour.
Our forebears rode together under one banner, yet here we are. Lay down your spear and spare our clans this grief.
My war-band is broken and my horse is spent. I yield to you, though it galls me to say it.
You let me ride free. I will remember it, though I make you no promise of friendship.
Take my sword, then. My lord will hear of this day, and the East forgets nothing.
You free an enemy who has sworn to destroy you. The East will not thank you, and neither will I.
You fought as our elders taught us, and I am beaten. I give you my sword with my clan's honour still on it.
Freed by one of my own blood. When our clans gather again, I will tell them of this.
By your leave, I return to my riders. Send for me and the war-band will come.
Go in peace while the peace holds. May your road be dry and your horses sound.
Keep your distance from my camp, and we will keep ours from yours.
Ride on. The steppe is wide, but my riders know every hoofprint on it.
May the grass be green wherever you ride. My fire is yours whenever you return.
We have watched for your coming through many nights. Our bows and our counsel are yours to command, my liege.
My liege, the road brings you back to us. Speak, and we will hear you as we have heard few others.
We know of you, though we have not met. Our realm keeps peace with yours, and we will keep it while you do.
Well met again under open sky. Friendship is rare in these waning days, and we do not spend it lightly.
You ride where our scouts have marked your passing for some days. State your purpose plainly; our patience is long, though it has an end.
We meet again at the edge of our lands. We remember every road you have taken near our borders, and we have not yet decided what they mean.
You stand before an old people with a long memory. Of those who came against us in arms, few are remembered by anyone but us.
We have not forgotten our last meeting. Nothing is forgotten among us, least of all the harm done to our realm.
The starlight finds us both on this road. It gladdens the heart to meet one of our own so far from the trees of home.
Again our paths cross, and the years between are as nothing. Come, share what you have seen since we parted.
Our arrows are on the string and your company is ringed about. Lay down your arms, and no blood need stain this ground.
You have wandered too long where you were not welcome. Yield to us now, and you will be treated with more grace than you have shown.
We held this land against darker enemies long before your line began. Yield, or fall here on this field.
You are surrounded, and our archers do not miss twice. Cast down your weapons and live to see another dawn.
It grieves us to draw bows against one of our own, yet we will. Yield, and let there be no kinslaying this day.
Our people have shed one another's blood before, and wept for it through long ages. Put up your sword and spare us that sorrow again.
We lower our bows. Our lives are in your keeping now.
You show more grace than we looked for. We will remember this, as we remember all things.
Our strength is spent and the field is lost. We yield, though the stars will see this end with sorrow.
You set us free, yet nothing of what lies between our peoples is mended. Go, before we think better of our thanks.
Enough. We will not fight our own kin to the last. Take our swords; we yield to you.
You remember what we share, even now. Let this mercy stand between us when the Sea calls us home.
Your will is ours to carry out. May the stars watch over your road, my liege.
Go in peace. The paths of friends cross again sooner than one expects.
Take your leave, and keep your distance from our borders. We will be watching.
Go from our sight. The trees will tell us where you walk.
Farewell, until our roads meet once more. The light grows dim in Middle-earth, but not so dim that friends lose each other.
My liege. The forges of my hold burn at your word, and every axe in it is yours to call.
Back on the road, my liege. The clans are glad of your rule, and your enemies grow fewer for it.
You come openly, so I will speak openly. We keep faith with those who keep faith with us, and we keep count as well.
We meet again. Your name stands well in our ledgers so far. See that it stays there.
I have heard your name spoken in our halls, and seldom kindly. Say what you want and be brief.
You again. Every slight you have done us is cut into stone, and stone keeps well.
Stand where you are. Your cause is the enemy of the halls of my people, and I have sworn on my grandsires' tombs to answer it.
Last we met you cost us dear, and that debt is written down in stone. We have outlasted worse enemies than you.
Well met, cousin. It warms the heart to see a face from the deep halls this far from the forges.
Hail again, cousin. There is ale in the wagon and news from home, if you can spare the time to hear it.
Your road ends at my shield-wall. Lay down your arms and you will be held fairly until your ransom is paid in full.
There is no quarrel between us worth dying for. Yield now and we will settle the matter in gold.
Throw down your weapons. Our halls have waited long to see you in chains, and I would sooner bring you in alive.
Yield, or be buried where you stand. The mountain takes the dead of our enemies and gives back nothing.
Put up your axe, cousin. I have no wish to shed the blood of our own line over this, but I will if you force it.
Lay down your arms. Our clans can mend this with gold and oaths, and there is no mending a split skull.
Enough. I yield, and I will pay what my ransom is worth. Reckon it fairly, for I will check your sums.
Freed without ransom? Then I owe you a debt, and I always pay my debts.
I yield, though it galls me past words. My kin will remember the price of it.
You set me loose. The war stands as it was, yet this one deed I will mark in your favour.
I yield to you, cousin. Let the shame of it stay within the clans, where such things belong.
Unbound by your own hand, cousin. My clan will hear of this, and they will count it to your honour.
By your leave, then. My hold stands ready whenever you call on it.
Safe roads to you. May your dealings with us stay as honest as they have been.
Go, then. And mind whose halls you trouble.
Get gone while I allow it. Next time the axes will do my talking.
Stone beneath your feet, cousin, and fire in your forge.
Great One! We heard you were on the road and the whole band ran ahead to clear it. Say the word and heads roll for you.
Back again, Great One, and every whip in my band still cracks in your name. Nobody here has slacked since last time, I made sure of it.
Hold your spears, you lot, this one is no enemy of ours today. Stay where my scouts can see you and we'll get along fine.
You again. Last time you kept your word and nobody got stabbed, so I call that a good start.
Stop right there. We may serve the same masters, but my band sharpens its knives on strangers all the same.
Back sniffing round my road, are you? I remember your face, and I remember who grabbed the last share.
Well, look what crawled out of the bushes. Fresh meat, and it came to us on its own feet.
You again, maggot. Last time you got lucky, and my cook has kept the pot warm ever since.
Ha, a proper face for once, scarred and ugly as the rest of us. Sit by the fire if you can stand the smell.
Still alive, you old gutter-rat? Grab a bone, there's meat left on this one.
Same masters or no, you've crossed my band once too often. Throw down your blades, or we settle it the old way.
Stand still and drop your gear. Behave, and I'll tell the overseers you came in quietly.
Nowhere to run, dung-crawler, we've sniffed you out. Throw your iron in the dirt and maybe you'll live long enough to dig in the pits.
Down on your knees and hand over your weapons. Fight us, and the pack eats well tonight.
Drop it, scum. You know how it goes: the stronger band takes the spoils, and today that's mine.
Yield now and I'll only take your boots and your share. Make me fight for it and I'll have your hide as well.
Enough, enough! Take what you want and we'll call it square. The masters can sort out the grudge later.
Letting me go? Huh. I won't forget it, and I won't forgive it either.
All right, put the blade down, I yield! A live captive fetches a better price than a corpse.
Soft, that's what you are, and soft things get trampled. Next time we meet I won't be so careless.
Ugh, you win, curse your teeth. Take the spoils and let me crawl off with what's left of my band.
You let me walk? Daft, but I'll remember it. Next time I catch you short, maybe I'll let you keep your ears.
Your will, Great One. If anyone in my band slacks, I'll flog them bloody myself.
Off you go, then. Keep clear of my scouts after dark, they stab first and sniff after.
Get gone. Turn your back near my camp for too long and see what happens.
Run along, worm. The road is long and my band is hungry.
Go on, then, and watch out for the whips. They're always looking for someone to blame.
